# Sampling and Weighting {#sec-sampling}

Part III turns from what each example looks like to which examples the model sees, and how much
each one counts. Two levers do this: the sampling distribution $q$ and the per-example weights
$w$. They are the same two levers that [rl-for-llms](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/rl-for-llms/chapters/02-policy-gradients.html)
uses to describe every policy-gradient method. Here they describe class rebalancing, prior
correction, importance weighting and synthetic oversampling. This chapter derives what each one
does to the learned probabilities, shows that resampling and reweighting aim at the same
target, and measures what they cost.

## The problem

A fraud detector trains on transactions in which 1 in 20 is fraud; a disease screen, on
patients of whom few are sick. Common advice says to balance the classes: undersample the
majority, weight the minority up, or synthesize minority examples. What does the model then
learn, and does it still estimate the probability the deployment needs? And when the inputs
seen in training differ from those met in deployment, can weights make up the difference?

## Assumptions

1. **Prior shift.** Rebalancing changes the class proportions and nothing else:
   $q(x \mid y) = p(x \mid y)$. This holds when examples are chosen by their label only. Saerens
   et al. state this condition [@saerens2002adjusting, §2.2], and it is what King and Zeng call
   choice-based sampling [@king2001logistic].
2. **Covariate shift.** For importance weighting, inputs are drawn differently but labels follow
   the same rule, $q(y \mid x) = p(y \mid x)$. Wherever $p(x) > 0$, also $q(x) > 0$, and the
   density ratio $w(x) = p(x)/q(x)$ is known. The
   [next chapter but one](10-distribution-shift.qmd#sec-shift) treats the case where it must be
   estimated.
3. **A well-specified, flexible enough model.** The demonstrations use logistic regression on
   T1, whose true posterior is logistic, so differences come from the data, not the model.

## Derivation or demonstration

**What balancing does to the posterior.** By Bayes' rule, a model trained where class $y$ has
prior $q(y)$ learns $q(y \mid x) \propto p(x \mid y)\, q(y)$, while the target is
$p(y \mid x) \propto p(x \mid y)\, p(y)$. Under assumption 1 the likelihoods cancel in the
ratio:

$$
p(y \mid x) = \frac{q(y \mid x)\, p(y)/q(y)}{\sum_{y'} q(y' \mid x)\, p(y')/q(y')}.
$$

This is Saerens et al.'s eq. 4: the posterior under training conditions, "weighted by the
ratio of the new priors to the old priors" and renormalized [@saerens2002adjusting]. For a
logistic model it reduces to King and Zeng's prior correction: subtract
$\ln\big[\tfrac{1-\tau}{\tau}\,\tfrac{\bar y}{1-\bar y}\big]$ from the intercept, where $\tau$
is the population fraction of ones and $\bar y$ the sample's [@king2001logistic, eq. 7]. A test
confirms that the two corrections agree to machine precision
(`tests/test_imbalance.py::test_king_zeng_intercept_correction_equals_saerens_for_logit`).

On T1 with {{< var ch8.prior_pct >}}% positives (30 seeds, 20,000 examples each), a plain logistic
regression's predicted probabilities sat on average {{< var ch8.plain_err >}} from the true
posterior. Trained on a balanced undersample, the distance rose to
{{< var ch8.under_err >}}; with balanced class weights, {{< var ch8.weighted_err >}}. After the
correction from a training prior of 1/2 back to the true prior, the distances were
{{< var ch8.under_corr_err >}} and {{< var ch8.weighted_corr_err >}}
(`tests/test_imbalance.py::test_prior_shift_correction_restores_calibration`).

::: {.callout-note title="Result: rebalancing changes the probabilities, not the ranking"}
Training with class priors $q(y)$ instead of $p(y)$, by resampling or by weighting, makes the
model learn $q(y \mid x)$, the true posterior tilted by $q(y)/p(y)$. Multiplying the output by
$p(y)/q(y)$ and renormalizing undoes the tilt exactly. At a threshold of 1/2, a model trained
on balanced classes decides as the true posterior would at a threshold equal to the true prior
(`tests/test_imbalance.py::test_balanced_threshold_at_one_half_is_the_prior_threshold`).
:::

So "balance the classes" and "lower the threshold" are the same decision rule. The first
changes the data and also destroys calibration; the second changes only the rule.

**Same target, different variance.** Undersampling pulls the $q$ lever: it discards majority
examples. Class weights pull the $w$ lever: they keep every example and count the minority
more. Both lead to the same tilted posterior. Over 30 seeds the coefficient on $z_1$ averaged
{{< var ch8.under_coef_mean >}} with undersampling and {{< var ch8.weighted_coef_mean >}} with
weights; the truth is 1.5. Its standard deviation across seeds was
{{< var ch8.under_coef_sd >}} with undersampling and {{< var ch8.weighted_coef_sd >}} with weights
(`tests/test_imbalance.py::test_resampling_and_reweighting_share_a_target_not_a_variance`). The
lever decides the variance, not the target.

{{< include ../includes/cards/balanced-resampling.md >}}

{{< include ../includes/cards/class-weights.md >}}

**When the target prior is unknown.** A model is deployed where the class mix has changed by an
unknown amount. If only the prior changed, Saerens et al. estimate it from the unlabeled new
data by EM. They start from the training prior, correct the posteriors to the current estimate
with eq. 4, and set the next estimate to the corrected posteriors' average (their eq. 9),
until it stops moving. On T1, with a model trained at prior 0.5 and 5,000 unlabeled examples
drawn at prior 0.1, the estimate averaged {{< var ch8.em_mean >}} over 20 seeds and ranged
from {{< var ch8.em_min >}} to {{< var ch8.em_max >}}
(`tests/test_imbalance.py::test_em_prior_estimation_recovers_test_prior`).

{{< include ../includes/cards/prior-shift-correction.md >}}

**Importance weighting.** Under covariate shift, labels follow the same rule but inputs are
drawn from $q$ instead of $p$. Any average under $p$ can then be written as a weighted average
under $q$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{p}[\ell] = \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[w(x)\,\ell\big], \qquad w(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} .
$$

The weighted sample mean is therefore unbiased. Its variance is
$\big(\mathbb{E}_q[w^2 \ell^2] - R^2\big)/n$, and $\mathbb{E}_q[w^2]$ grows quickly with the
shift. For Gaussian $q = \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$ and $p = \mathcal{N}(\delta, \Sigma)$, it equals
$\exp(\delta^\top \Sigma^{-1} \delta)$. On T1, estimating the risk of a fixed classifier under
$p$ from 1,000 examples of $q$, the weighted estimate was unbiased at every shift: at the
largest, it averaged {{< var ch8.iw_mean_last >}} against an exact {{< var ch8.iw_truth_last >}}.
The unweighted estimate stayed at {{< var ch8.naive_mean >}}. The standard deviation of the
weighted estimate grew from {{< var ch8.iw_sd_first >}} to {{< var ch8.iw_sd_last >}}, as
$\mathbb{E}_q[w^2]$ grew from 1 to {{< var ch8.w2_last >}}. The variance is known in closed
form here, and its value lay inside the bootstrap interval of the measured variance at every
shift (`tests/test_shift.py::test_importance_weighting_unbiased_with_growing_variance`).

::: {.callout-important title="Lineage: this is importance sampling"}
Writing an average under $p$ as a weighted average under $q$ is importance sampling.
Weighting a model's training loss by $p(x)/q(x)$ to correct covariate shift goes back at least
to Shimodaira's 2000 paper, whose title states the method: improving predictive inference
under covariate shift by weighting the log-likelihood function [@shimodaira2000improving; only
its bibliographic record could be read for this book]. `rl-for-llms` uses the same pair
$(q, w)$ for reinforcement learning
([rl-for-llms, The Map](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/rl-for-llms/chapters/00-map.html)).
:::

{{< include ../includes/cards/importance-weighting.md >}}

**Synthetic minority examples.** SMOTE oversamples the minority class by "taking each minority
class sample and introducing synthetic examples along the line segments joining any/all of the
k minority class nearest neighbors" [@chawla2002smote, §4.2]. Each synthetic point is a minority
example plus a uniform fraction of the difference to one of its neighbors. It assumes the space
between nearby minority examples belongs to the minority class.

{{< include ../includes/cards/smote.md >}}

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
scikit-learn's `class_weight="balanced"` sets each class's weight to
`n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))` (scikit-learn 1.9). The rebalanced model's
`predict_proba` is then tilted; correct it with the prior ratio, or keep the plain model and
choose the threshold the decision needs. Resample or synthesize inside each training fold, never
before splitting ([Cleaning](04-cleaning.qmd#sec-cleaning)).
:::

## What it does to the learned model

Rebalancing does not teach the model anything new about the minority class. It changes the
prior the model believes in. The ranking of examples, and hence any threshold-free metric,
is unchanged in expectation. The probabilities are inflated by a known factor that can be
removed. What rebalancing does change is the variance, through the lever used: discarding
examples costs precision, and weighting does not.

Importance weighting changes the target from $q$ to $p$ at a price paid in effective sample
size. At the largest shift here, 1,000 weighted examples estimate the risk under $p$ about as
precisely as {{< var ch8.n_eff_last >}} unweighted examples drawn from $p$ itself would: the
weighted estimate's exact variance equals that of a plain average of about that many losses.

## Failure modes

![Panel A: on T1 with 5% positives, predicted probability against the true posterior, for a plain model, one trained on a balanced undersample, one with balanced class weights, and the undersampled model after prior correction. Panel B: the coefficient on $z_1$ over 30 seeds, undersampling against class weights (truth 1.5). Panel C: importance-weighted and unweighted estimates of the risk under a shifted $p$ from 1,000 examples of $q$, against the exact risk (500 seeds). Panel D: share of SMOTE's synthetic points in the gap between the two clusters of a 20-example minority class, by neighbor count (50 seeds). Balancing tilts probabilities in a correctable way; the lever sets the variance; importance weights trade bias for variance; SMOTE fills gaps once $k$ exceeds a cluster.](../images/sampling_weighting.png){#fig-sampling-weighting}

@fig-sampling-weighting shows the four effects. The failure modes:

- **Uncorrected probabilities.** A rebalanced model used where probabilities matter (pricing,
  triage, combining with other evidence) overstates the minority class at every input (panel A).
- **Weights that explode.** Importance weights are heavy-tailed when $q$ is thin where $p$ is
  not. At the largest shift, the bootstrap interval for the estimator's own variance spans a
  factor of {{< var ch8.boot_ratio_last >}} (panel C): even its precision is hard to measure. An estimated density ratio, which practice requires, adds its
  own error where data is sparse.
- **SMOTE across gaps.** With 20 minority examples split into two separated clusters, SMOTE with
  up to 5 neighbors put {{< var ch8.smote_gap_k5 >}}% of its synthetic points in the gap between
  them, against a true {{< var ch8.smote_true_gap >}}%. With 15 neighbors, more than a cluster
  holds, it put {{< var ch8.smote_gap_k15 >}}% there
  (`tests/test_imbalance.py::test_smote_fills_the_gap_when_k_exceeds_cluster_size`). Those
  points are minority labels in majority territory.
- **A prior shift that is not one.** If $p(x \mid y)$ also changed (a new kind of fraud, not more
  of the old kind), eq. 4 and EM correct the wrong thing.

## What the toy cannot show

T1's posterior is exactly logistic, its density ratio is known in closed form, and its
minority clusters are Gaussian. Real class-conditional distributions change along with the
priors, density ratios must be estimated, and the geometry of a minority class is unknown. The
demonstrations show what each lever targets and what it costs, not how well a given estimate of
a prior or a ratio will work on real data.

  known probability is undone by the same $1/s$ weights; importance weighting is that idea
  under covariate shift.
- [Labels](02-labels.qmd#sec-labels): the noisy-label posterior is also a known transform of the
